plants.ingestionRisk: Toxic to dogs if eaten; plant contact may also cause dermatitis in some animals.
plants.summary: Flat white flower clusters and finely divided, feathery leaves; safe to pass, but do not let dogs chew it.
plants.elevation: Valley floor to alpine grassland, depending on locality
identification: Many tiny white or pale-pink flower heads form a broad, flat-topped cluster
Leaves are narrow and divided into many fine, feathery segments
Stems are upright and usually lightly hairy
lookalikes: Wild carrot and other white-flowered umbellifers; check the flower-head structure and leaves carefully
plants.dogSafety: Normal proximity and sniffing are not expected to cause poisoning. Ingestion can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, depression, increased urination or dermatitis.
actionIfIngested: Move the dog away and prevent further chewing
Photograph the whole plant and close details; keep a small sample only if it can be collected safely and legally
Call your veterinarian promptly for advice, especially if symptoms appear or the amount is unknown
Do not induce vomiting or give home remedies unless a veterinary professional instructs you
plants.interestingFact: The genus name refers to Achilles, who was traditionally associated with using the plant on wounds; that history does not make the plant safe for dogs to eat.

image.alt: Common yarrow with flat clusters of tiny white flowers and feathery leaves

plants.ingestionRisk: Roses are classed as non-toxic to dogs, but thorns can injure and any plant material may upset the stomach if eaten.
plants.summary: Five-petalled pink or white flowers on thorny shrubs; non-toxic, with a physical hazard from prickles.
plants.elevation: Lower valleys to montane slopes, varying by species
identification: Usually five pink or white petals around a yellow centre
Compound leaves with toothed leaflets
Arching stems armed with prickles
Red or orange hips develop after flowering
lookalikes: Bramble species; flowers and fruits differ, but both can snag fur and skin
plants.dogSafety: No systemic toxicity is expected from roses. Keep dogs out of dense thorny growth and discourage eating hips, seeds or foliage because choking, mouth injury or stomach upset is still possible.
symptoms: possible mild stomach upset after ingestion
actionIfIngested: If only a small amount was eaten and the dog is well, monitor and contact your veterinarian if symptoms develop
Seek veterinary help for persistent vomiting, pain, choking, eye injury or a thorn embedded in skin
Do not induce vomiting unless directed by a veterinary professional
plants.interestingFact: Rose hips persist beyond the flowers and provide winter food for wildlife.

image.alt: Wild rose shrub with five-petalled pink flowers, toothed leaves and prickly stems

plants.ingestionRisk: Classed as non-toxic to dogs; eating plant material can still cause gastrointestinal upset.
plants.summary: Tight rosettes of thick pointed leaves on dry, rocky ground; non-toxic, but not a trail snack.
plants.elevation: Montane and subalpine rocky sites; also widely cultivated
identification: Dense rosettes of fleshy, pointed leaves
Rosettes produce smaller offsets around the parent
Mature rosettes may send up a tall stalk of star-shaped pinkish flowers
lookalikes: Other succulent rosettes; cultivated plants may occur near settlements
plants.dogSafety: Normal contact is low risk and the plant is classed as non-toxic. Prevent repeated grazing because any plant material may trigger vomiting or diarrhoea.
symptoms: possible mild vomiting or diarrhoea after eating plant material
actionIfIngested: Remove access and monitor
Call your veterinarian if a large amount was eaten or any symptom persists
Do not induce vomiting unless directed by a veterinary professional
plants.interestingFact: Its name Sempervivum means “always living,” a nod to the hardy evergreen rosettes.

image.alt: Hens and chicks forming clusters of fleshy pointed leaf rosettes on rock

evidence.label: ASPCA — Hens and chicks listed as non-toxic

plants.ingestionRisk: Fresh plants contain irritant compounds and are toxic to dogs if chewed or swallowed.
plants.summary: Glossy yellow flowers common in damp grass; safe to walk past, irritating if chewed.
plants.elevation: Valleys to alpine turf, depending on species
identification: Usually five glossy yellow petals
Green centre with many stamens
Leaves are often divided or lobed; form varies greatly by species
lookalikes: Marsh marigold and other yellow flowers; do not identify from colour alone
plants.dogSafety: Chewing fresh buttercups can irritate the mouth and digestive tract. Normal walking nearby is not a poisoning risk.
actionIfIngested: Stop further chewing and move away from the patch
Call your veterinarian if plant material was swallowed or symptoms appear
Do not induce vomiting or give home remedies unless directed by a veterinary professional
plants.interestingFact: The familiar shine comes from the flower's unusual petal structure, which reflects light strongly.

image.alt: Buttercup with glossy five-petalled yellow flowers in damp grass

plants.ingestionRisk: The main trail hazard is contact with stinging hairs; mouthing can irritate the lips and mouth.
plants.summary: Opposite toothed leaves covered in stinging hairs; avoid face, paw and skin contact.
plants.elevation: Valley and montane sites, often near human or livestock activity
identification: Opposite, pointed leaves with sharply toothed edges
Square-ish upright stems
Fine stinging hairs on leaves and stems
Small greenish flower clusters hang from leaf joints
plants.dogSafety: Brushing against nettles can cause temporary pain, redness and licking, especially on sparsely haired areas. Eye or mouth exposure deserves extra caution.
actionIfIngested: Lead the dog away and prevent rubbing the face
Seek veterinary advice for eye exposure, facial swelling, breathing difficulty, marked pain or persistent symptoms
Do not apply creams or medicines unless your veterinarian recommends them
plants.interestingFact: The hollow hairs act like tiny needles that deliver irritating chemicals when broken.

image.alt: Stinging nettle with opposite toothed leaves and fine hairs on upright stems

evidence.label: ASPCA — Toxic and non-toxic plant list (general limitations)

plants.ingestionRisk: All parts contain potent alkaloids; ingestion is a veterinary emergency.
plants.summary: Tall spikes of deep blue-violet hooded flowers; one of the highest-priority plants to prevent dogs from chewing.
identification: Deep blue to purple flowers shaped like a hood or helmet
Flowers arranged on a tall upright spike
Dark green leaves deeply divided into narrow lobes
lookalikes: Larkspur and other blue flower spikes; treat an uncertain identification as dangerous
plants.dogSafety: Walking past or sniffing without chewing is not expected to poison a dog. Any suspected bite or ingestion needs immediate veterinary advice; do not wait for symptoms.
actionIfIngested: Call the nearest veterinarian or emergency clinic immediately and start travelling if advised
Prevent further exposure; use gloves if collecting a sample and do not handle the face
Take photos and note the time and possible amount
Do not induce vomiting or give food, drink, charcoal or medication unless instructed by a veterinary professional
plants.interestingFact: The helmet-like upper sepal gives monkshood its English name.

image.alt: Monkshood with a tall spike of deep violet helmet-shaped flowers and divided leaves

evidence.label: Merck Veterinary Manual — Plants poisonous to animals

plants.ingestionRisk: Extremely toxic; all parts are hazardous and even small ingestions can be serious.
plants.summary: Pink-lilac crocus-like flowers appearing from the ground in autumn, often without leaves; ingestion is an emergency.
identification: Pink to lilac goblet-shaped flowers usually appear in late summer or autumn
Flowers often emerge without visible leaves
Broad leaves and seed capsule appear in spring
lookalikes: Spring crocus; flowering time helps but is not enough for a safe identification
plants.dogSafety: Do not let a dog mouth any part. Toxicity may involve the digestive tract, heart, liver, kidneys, blood and bone marrow; effects can be delayed.
actionIfIngested: Treat any suspected ingestion as an emergency and contact a veterinarian immediately
Do not wait for symptoms, which may be delayed
Photograph the plant and note the time and amount if known
Do not induce vomiting or give home remedies unless instructed by a veterinary professional
plants.interestingFact: Despite its common name, it is not a true Crocus; it belongs to a different plant family.

image.alt: Autumn crocus with leafless pink-lilac goblet flowers emerging in meadow grass

evidence.label: Merck Veterinary Manual — Plants poisonous to animals

plants.ingestionRisk: Rhododendron species contain grayanotoxins; ingestion of only a few leaves can cause serious illness.
plants.summary: Evergreen mountain shrubs with clusters of vivid pink flowers; every part should be kept out of a dog's mouth.
habitats: acid or limestone sites depending on species
identification: Low evergreen shrub forming broad patches
Clusters of bright pink, funnel-shaped flowers
Leathery narrow leaves; underside characters differ between the two Alpine species
lookalikes: Cultivated azaleas and other Rhododendron species, which should also be treated as toxic
plants.dogSafety: All parts are considered toxic. Ingestion can affect digestion, the nervous system and the heart. Safe to pass on trail, but keep dogs from biting leaves or flowers.
actionIfIngested: Contact a veterinarian immediately; do not wait for symptoms
Remove any loose plant fragments only if this can be done safely without pushing material deeper
Take photos and note the time and possible amount
Do not induce vomiting or give remedies unless instructed by a veterinary professional
plants.interestingFact: The two classic Alpine alpenroses favour different geology, but both belong to the toxic Rhododendron genus.

image.alt: Alpine rhododendron forming a low evergreen shrub with vivid pink flower clusters

plants.ingestionRisk: All parts contain cardiac glycosides; ingestion can disrupt heart function.
plants.summary: Tall one-sided spikes of tubular, spotted bells; highly toxic if eaten.
plants.elevation: Lower valleys to montane sites; often naturalised
identification: Tall spike with many hanging tubular flowers
Flowers usually purple-pink with darker spots inside, sometimes white
Large soft, wrinkled leaves form a basal rosette
lookalikes: Other Digitalis species; treat all as dangerous
Comfrey before flowering; never rely on leaves alone
plants.dogSafety: All parts are poisonous. Cardiac glycosides have a narrow margin of safety, so suspected ingestion is urgent even before symptoms appear.
actionIfIngested: Call a veterinarian or emergency clinic immediately
Photograph the plant and note exposure time and amount
Keep the dog calm and follow professional instructions
Do not induce vomiting or give remedies unless a veterinary professional directs you
plants.interestingFact: Digitalis medicines originated from foxglove compounds, but the plant itself has an unpredictable and dangerous dose.

image.alt: Foxglove with a tall one-sided spike of purple-pink spotted tubular flowers

evidence.label: Merck Veterinary Manual — cardiac glycoside plants

plants.ingestionRisk: Leaves, flowers, rhizomes and even vase water can contain cardiac glycosides.
plants.summary: Fragrant white bells above paired broad leaves; dangerous if any part is eaten.
identification: A one-sided arch of small, nodding white bell-shaped flowers
Two or three broad basal leaves
Orange-red berries may follow later in the season
lookalikes: Wild garlic before flowering; crushing leaves to smell them is not a safe dog-identification method
Solomon's seal, which carries bells beneath an arched leafy stem
plants.dogSafety: All parts should be treated as poisonous. Cardiac effects make suspected ingestion urgent.
actionIfIngested: Contact a veterinarian immediately
Take photos; safely keep packaging or a plant sample if exposure came from a bouquet
Do not wait for symptoms
Do not induce vomiting or give remedies unless directed by a veterinary professional
plants.interestingFact: Its underground rhizomes can create dense colonies, so many visible shoots may be connected.

image.alt: Lily of the valley with small white bells on an arched stem between broad leaves

evidence.label: Merck Veterinary Manual — cardiac glycoside plants

plants.ingestionRisk: Needles, bark and seeds contain taxines; poisoning may progress rapidly and sudden death is possible.
plants.summary: Dark evergreen tree or shrub with flat needles and red fleshy arils; a critical ingestion hazard.
identification: Flat, dark green evergreen needles arranged along the twig
Red cup-like fleshy arils around a hard seed in late summer or autumn
Reddish-brown, flaky bark on older stems
lookalikes: Fir and other conifers; the red arils are distinctive but should never be handled as food
plants.dogSafety: Do not allow chewing of any yew material or scavenging beneath clipped hedges. The red flesh itself is described as non-poisonous, but the enclosed seed is toxic, so the whole structure is unsafe for dogs.
actionIfIngested: Seek emergency veterinary help immediately, even if the dog looks normal
Bring photos and note whether needles, twigs or red arils may be involved
Do not induce vomiting or give remedies unless directed by a veterinary professional
plants.interestingFact: Yews can live for many centuries, which is one reason they are strongly associated with historic sites.

image.alt: European yew with flat dark needles, reddish bark and red cup-like arils

evidence.label: ASPCA — Western yew (Taxus toxicity and clinical signs)

plants.ingestionRisk: All parts are toxic, with bulbs usually posing the greatest risk.
plants.summary: Spring flowers with a central trumpet; common near settlements and pastures, and toxic if eaten.
plants.elevation: Mainly lower valleys and montane settlements; often planted or naturalised
identification: Six petal-like segments surrounding a central trumpet or cup
Narrow strap-shaped leaves rise from a bulb
Flowers are often yellow or white
lookalikes: Other spring bulbs, some of which are also toxic
plants.dogSafety: Prevent digging around bulbs and chewing flowers or leaves. Bulbs are especially concentrated and may also cause obstruction if swallowed.
symptoms: abnormal heart rhythm in severe cases
actionIfIngested: Call your veterinarian promptly; treat bulb ingestion or symptoms as urgent
Photograph the plant and estimate the part and amount eaten
Do not induce vomiting or give home remedies unless directed by a veterinary professional
plants.interestingFact: Many daffodils seen beside Alpine villages are naturalised garden plants rather than truly wild populations.

image.alt: Yellow daffodil with six outer segments and a central trumpet above narrow leaves

plants.ingestionRisk: Insoluble calcium oxalate crystals cause immediate, intense irritation of the mouth and throat.
plants.summary: Arrow-shaped leaves, a hooded spring flower and a later spike of orange-red berries; biting it can cause severe oral pain and swelling.
identification: Large arrow-shaped leaves, sometimes dark-spotted
Pale green hood encloses a purple-brown central spike in spring
A bare spike of bright orange-red berries appears later
plants.dogSafety: Chewing usually causes immediate pain, drooling and pawing at the mouth. Swelling near the airway can become urgent.
actionIfIngested: Remove access and contact a veterinarian
Seek emergency care immediately for tongue/throat swelling or breathing difficulty
Do not induce vomiting; do not give food, drink or medication unless a veterinary professional directs you
plants.interestingFact: Its conspicuous autumn berry spike appears after the spring leaves and flower have faded, making the same plant look very different through the year.

image.alt: Lords-and-ladies with arrow-shaped leaves and a pale green hood around a dark central spike

evidence.label: ASPCA — Arum maculatum listed as toxic
